1. Axe du programme

Programme d’anglais du lycée général et technologique, BO n° 22 du 29 mai 2025, en vigueur en Première et en Terminale depuis la rentrée 2026.

ClasseAxe principalAxes possibles aussi
PremièreAxe 3. Art et pouvoir. Hamlet se sert du théâtre pour démasquer un roi : « The play’s the thing / Wherein I’ll catch the conscience of the king » ; l’art devient une arme contre un pouvoir corrompu.Axe 1. Identités et échanges : la pièce anglaise la plus jouée et traduite au monde, un patrimoine partagé que chaque époque réinvente (Maclise en 1842, le cinéma aujourd’hui).
TerminaleAxe 3. Fictions et réalités. Un spectre, une folie jouée et une pièce dans la pièce brouillent la frontière entre l’illusion et le vrai.Axe 1. Espace privé et espace public : un crime de famille empoisonne tout l’État, « Something is rotten in the state of Denmark ». Axe 4. Enjeux et formes de la communication : le monologue, l’espionnage, la mise en scène de la vérité.

2. Problématique

What makes Hamlet a tragic hero? Qu’est-ce qui fait d’Hamlet un héros tragique ?

Lesson 1: Why is a ghost the perfect start for a tragedy? · Lesson 2: Should Hamlet obey the ghost? · Lesson 3: Is Hamlet mad, or does he only act mad? · Lesson 4: What does Hamlet’s most famous speech tell us about the tragic hero? · Lesson 5: Why does everybody die, and what remains?

3. Objectifs linguistiques

  • Modals of deduction: must, might, can’t; must have + past participle (lesson 1).
  • Obligation and moral judgement: should, ought to, have to, must not; should have (lesson 2).
  • Reported speech: said that, told, asked if (lesson 3).
  • Hypothesis: if, whether … or, unless, what if (lesson 4).
  • Linking words for a critical paragraph: because, because of, therefore, whereas, although, despite (lesson 5).
  • Language activities : compréhension de l’écrit (extraits de la pièce), expression orale en continu (monologue moderne), interaction orale (jeux de rôle), expression écrite (le récit d’Horatio).

4. Ancrage culturel

La tragédie de vengeance élisabéthaine (Shakespeare, vers 1600, le théâtre du Globe) ; le tragique selon Aristote (hamartia, pitié et crainte) ; Hamlet peint par l’époque victorienne (Maclise, 1842) ; Hamlet aujourd’hui au théâtre et au cinéma.

5. Niveau CECRL

  • Première : B1+ vers B2.
  • Terminale LV1 : B2 vers C1, avec un parcours C1/C2 à chaque lesson.
  • Bac pro (Version B) : B1, quatre lessons.
  • Dys-friendly version : B1, quatre lessons, une étape à la fois.

Lesson 1: The ghost on the walls

Part 1. Why is a ghost the perfect start for a tragedy?

Objectives

  • Discover the plot and the characters
  • Describe a supernatural scene
  • Use modals of deduction (must, might, can't)
Today's language goal

To present the play and its characters and describe a supernatural scene, we need the words of the plot (ghost, revenge, crown, poison, court, castle) and the modals of deduction (The ghost must be his father).

Getting started

Lights off. Students hear the word ghost and list everything it suggests: fear, the past, unfinished business. Why do ghosts come back in stories?

Documents

Document: the play. Hamlet is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, written around 1600. Prince Hamlet of Denmark comes home after his father's death. His uncle Claudius is now king and has married Hamlet's mother, Gertrude. A ghost appears on the walls of the castle of Elsinore: it is Hamlet's father, who says Claudius poisoned him. Hamlet must decide whether to believe the ghost and take revenge. At the end, almost all the main characters die: Polonius, Ophelia, Laertes, Gertrude, Claudius and Hamlet himself. Only his friend Horatio survives to tell the story.

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 1: The ghost on the walls

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act I, scenes 4 and 5

  • “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.” (Act I, scene 4, Marcellus)
  • “I am thy father's spirit, / Doom'd for a certain term to walk the night” (Act I, scene 5, the Ghost)
  • “Adieu, adieu, adieu! remember me.” (Act I, scene 5, the Ghost)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeI.4 and I.5What strikes you first?
A dead king speaks: “I am thy father's spirit” (I.5). Before that, a guard says: “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark” (I.4).
The play opens on something wrong, in the royal family and in the whole country.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesI.5Which clues? In which line?
“Doom'd for a certain term to walk the night” (I.5) and “remember me” (I.5), with “Adieu” said three times.
The words of night and doom make the ghost a messenger from death. His last wish is not only revenge: it is memory.
Quote each clue with its act and scene.
3 Je comprends · I understandI.4What effect? What contrast?
“Something is rotten in the state of Denmark” (I.4): a country cannot rot like fruit or meat.
The metaphor turns a secret crime into a public disease: the corruption at the top of the state will spread to everything.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictI.5, then II.2What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: Hamlet will obey the ghost and take revenge immediately.
Not confirmed: the ghost asks “remember me” (I.5), and in Act II Hamlet still wants proof: “The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king” (II.2).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningI.4 and I.5Which interpretation do I defend?
The ghost brings a secret from death into the court: “Something is rotten” (I.4), “remember me” (I.5).
From the first act, the hero is trapped between memory and action, between a duty and a doubt: this is where the tragic begins.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … scene … This shows me … because …”

Lesson 1: The ghost on the walls · Dys-friendly version

Question: Why is a ghost the perfect start for a tragedy?

Four words:

  • ghost: the spirit of a dead person
  • revenge: punishing someone for a wrong they did
  • uncle: your father's or mother's brother
  • poisoned: killed with a toxic substance

Steps: 1. Read the line aloud. 2. Learn the four words. 3. Do the spiral below, one step at a time. 4. Say your answer with the support sentence.

Grammar lesson: modals of deduction: must, might, can't (present and past)

To present the play and its characters and describe a supernatural scene, we need modals of deduction: must, might, can't (present and past)
For the teacher: how to run it (8 to 10 minutes)
  1. Read “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark”. Ask: what does Marcellus suspect? Collect guesses.
  2. Draw the certainty line: can't (no), might / could (maybe), must (yes). Students copy.
  3. Add the past: must have + past participle. “Claudius must have poisoned the king.” Ask what the clue is.
  4. Quick check, then exercises, then the character chart and the role play.
On the board, to copy

Rule

To make a guess from clues, use a modal + base verb for now, and a modal + have + past participle for the past. must = almost sure; might / could = possible; can't = almost sure it is not true.

Form

  • now: modal + base verb: The ghost must be Hamlet's father.
  • past: modal + have + past participle: Claudius must have poisoned him.
  • the negative of must (deduction) is can't: It can't be a dream.
  • questions: Could the ghost be lying?

Use

  • To talk about the ghost: real or imagined, honest or lying?
  • To guess what happened before the play starts.
  • Always add the clue: because, since, so.

Examples from the lesson

  • The ghost must be Hamlet's father: it wears his armour.
  • Claudius must have poisoned the king, if the ghost says the truth.
  • The ghost might be a devil who wants to trick Hamlet.
  • It can't be a dream: the guards saw it too.

Common mistakes

WrongRight
The ghost must to be his father.The ghost must be his father.
It mustn't be a dream.It can't be a dream.
Claudius must poisoned the king.Claudius must have poisoned the king.
Can the ghost lie? (deduction)Could the ghost be lying?

Quick check (2 minutes, hands up or mini whiteboards)Must, might or can't?

  1. The guards saw it too: it ______ be a dream.
  2. The ghost wears the king's armour: it ______ be the king.
  3. We have no proof: the ghost ______ be lying.
  4. Claudius ______ have killed his brother: the ghost says so.
Show the answers

1. can't. 2. must. 3. might. 4. must (or might, if we doubt the ghost).

Exercises

EntryRecognition. How sure is the speaker: yes (Y), maybe (M), no (N)? Now or past?

  1. Something must be wrong in Denmark.
  2. The ghost might be a devil.
  3. Claudius must have poisoned the king.
  4. Hamlet can't be happy about the wedding.
  5. Gertrude might not have known about the murder.
  6. It can't have been an accident.
Show the answers

1. Y, now. 2. M, now. 3. Y, past. 4. N, now. 5. M, past. 6. N, past.

CoreTransformation. Rewrite with must, might or can't (present or past).

  1. I'm sure the ghost is the old king.
  2. Perhaps Horatio is afraid.
  3. I'm sure Hamlet isn't happy at court.
  4. I'm sure Claudius killed his brother.
  5. Perhaps Gertrude didn't know.
  6. I'm sure it wasn't a natural death.
  7. Maybe the ghost is telling the truth.
Show the answers

1. The ghost must be the old king. 2. Horatio might be afraid. 3. Hamlet can't be happy at court. 4. Claudius must have killed his brother. 5. Gertrude might not have known. 6. It can't have been a natural death. 7. The ghost might be telling the truth.

StretchProduction. You are a guard on the walls. Write five deductions about the ghost and the king's death, each with a clue.

Show the answers

For example: The ghost wears the king's armour, so it must be the dead king. It only appears at night: it might be a spirit from purgatory. It can't be a dream, because three of us saw it. The king died suddenly; someone must have poisoned him. Claudius married the queen very fast: he might have planned everything.

Going further (for students heading to language studies)Advanced. Use the continuous and passive forms of deduction. Rewrite.

  1. Perhaps the ghost is waiting for Hamlet. (continuous)
  2. I'm sure someone poured poison into his ear. (passive past)
  3. I'm sure Hamlet has not been sleeping. (can't + continuous perfect)
Show the answers

1. The ghost might be waiting for Hamlet. 2. Poison must have been poured into his ear. 3. Hamlet can't have been sleeping. Continuous and passive forms let a critic make precise guesses about action and responsibility.

Words in action

To say it precisely, we need the right words

EntryMatch: ghost, revenge, crown, poison.

  1. a substance that kills
  2. the spirit of a dead person
  3. punishing someone for a wrong
  4. the symbol of a king's power
Show the answers

1. poison. 2. ghost. 3. revenge. 4. crown.

CoreComplete the plot with the character chart: Claudius is Hamlet's ______. Gertrude is his ______. Polonius is the ______ to the king. Horatio is Hamlet's ______.

Show the answers

uncle, mother, adviser, friend.

StretchDescribe the ghost scene in three sentences with: walls, night, spirit, remember.

Show the answers

For example: At night, on the walls of Elsinore, a ghost appears. It is the spirit of Hamlet's dead father. Before leaving, it asks Hamlet to remember him.

Activities

  1. Character map: Hamlet, Claudius, Gertrude, the Ghost, Horatio, Polonius, Ophelia, Laertes. Draw the links.
  2. Read the three quotations. Who speaks? What does the ghost want?
  3. Language: deduction. The ghost must be the old king. It might be a devil. It can't be a dream: three men saw it.
  4. Acting troupes: in groups of four, stage the ghost scene in one minute, with a narrator, Hamlet, Horatio and the Ghost.

More activities

Exercises
  1. Complete with must, might or can't: Horatio, Marcellus and Bernardo all saw the ghost, so it ______ be a dream.
  2. The ghost looks like the old king, so it ______ be his spirit.
  3. Hamlet is not sure: the ghost ______ be a devil trying to trick him.
  4. Find in the quotations a word meaning 'goodbye'.
  5. What is 'rotten' in Denmark, according to you?
Answer key: exercises
  1. can't
  2. must
  3. might
  4. adieu

Sentence starters

  • The ghost must be...
  • It might be...

Role play

Student A is Horatio, Student B is Hamlet. Horatio tells Hamlet what he saw on the walls last night. Hamlet asks questions.

Figures of speech in the documents

Metaphor: “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark”

“Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.” (Act I, scene 4, Marcellus)

A country cannot rot like fruit or meat: Marcellus compares Denmark to a body or a food that is going bad. This is a metaphor. It suggests a hidden corruption at the top of the state (the murder, the hasty marriage) which will spread to everything.

EntryWhat can be rotten in real life?

Show the answers

Food, fruit, meat, wood.

CoreWhat is rotten in Denmark, in fact?

Show the answers

The power: the king was murdered by his brother, who now sits on the throne and has married the queen.

StretchUse the same metaphor to describe a modern situation, then explain it.

Show the answers

For example: Something is rotten in this club: the best players never play. The metaphor suggests a hidden problem that spoils the whole group.

Expression task

Now say it

Role play: two guards on the walls of Elsinore at midnight see the ghost.

EntryEach guard says two sentences, one with must, might or can't.

CoreTwo minutes: describe the ghost, make three deductions, decide to tell Hamlet.

StretchUse a past deduction (must have) and the metaphor “something is rotten”.

Tools to use:

Show a model answer

A: Look, over there! It must be the old king: it wears his armour. B: It can't be a dream; Horatio saw it too. A: It might be a devil who wants to trick us. B: Or the king must have something to say. Something is rotten in the state of Denmark. A: We must tell Prince Hamlet tonight.

PREMIÈRE · UPPER SECONDARY · B1+ towards B2

Lesson 2: Revenge: duty or crime?

Part 2. Should Hamlet obey the ghost?

Objectives

  • Understand the revenge tragedy
  • Express obligation and moral judgment
  • Debate with arguments
Today's language goal

To weigh the arguments for and against revenge and give my judgement, we need the words of moral choice (duty, proof, conscience, sin, justice, guilty, trap) and should, ought to, have to, must not (and should have to judge the past).

Getting started

Vote with your feet: one side of the room for 'revenge is justice', the other for 'revenge is a crime'. Explain your choice in one sentence.

Documents

"Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder."
William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act I, scene 5, the Ghost
Document: revenge tragedy. In Elizabethan England, revenge plays were very popular. The law and the Church condemned private revenge, so the hero is caught between a sacred duty to his father and a sin.
"The play's the thing Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king."
William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act II, scene 2, Hamlet

Dilemma table

ChoiceForAgainst
Kill Claudius nowjustice for his fatherno proof, it is a sin
Test him with a playproof firsttime lost, danger
Do nothingno crimethe murderer keeps the crown

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 2: Revenge: duty or crime?

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act I, scene 5, and Act II, scene 2

  • “Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder.” (Act I, scene 5, the Ghost)
  • “The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king.” (Act II, scene 2, Hamlet)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeI.5What strikes you first?
The ghost's line starts with an imperative: “Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder” (I.5).
The first word is an order: a dead father gives a command to his living son.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesI.5 and II.2Which clues? In which line?
The father says “foul” and “most unnatural” (I.5). Hamlet says “catch” and “conscience” (II.2).
The father judges and condemns; the son prepares a trap and thinks about guilt.
Quote each clue with its act and scene.
3 Je comprends · I understandII.2What effect? What contrast?
Instead of a sword, Hamlet chooses a play: “The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king” (II.2). The rhyme thing / king closes the trap.
Hamlet answers violence with theatre: art becomes a weapon against power, a way to make the guilty king show his guilt.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictII.2, then V.2What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: if the play catches the king, Hamlet will kill him at once.
Partly confirmed: the plan is to “catch the conscience of the king” (II.2), but Hamlet kills Claudius only in the last scene (Act V, scene 2), after many deaths.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningI.5 and II.2Which interpretation do I defend?
“Revenge” (I.5) is a sacred duty to the father; “conscience” (II.2) reminds us that the law and the Church condemned private revenge.
Hamlet is caught between two laws: the duty to his father and the sin of killing. His conscience is his weapon and his obstacle.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … scene … This shows me … because …”

Vocabulary

WordMeaning

Grammar lesson: should, ought to, have to, must not; should have

To weigh the arguments for and against revenge and give my judgement, we need should, ought to, have to, must not; should have
For the teacher: how to run it (8 to 10 minutes)
  1. Read the Ghost's order: “Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder.” Ask: what does Hamlet have to do? What should he do?
  2. Distinguish on the board: have to (an obligation from outside, here the Ghost), should / ought to (a moral opinion), must not (forbidden by law or the Church). Students copy.
  3. Add should have + past participle to judge Hamlet's past choices.
  4. Quick check, then exercises, then the dilemma table and the troupe performance.
On the board, to copy

Rule

have to: an obligation imposed from outside. should / ought to: what is right in my opinion. must not: it is forbidden. should have + past participle: a judgement on a past action (it was a mistake not to do it).

Form

  • has to / have to + base verb: Hamlet has to find proof.
  • should / ought to + base verb: He should not believe the ghost immediately.
  • must not + base verb: A Christian must not kill.
  • should have + past participle: He should have acted earlier.

Use

  • To present the arguments for and against revenge.
  • To judge the characters' choices.
  • To build a debate: on the one hand he has to ..., on the other hand he must not ...

Examples from the lesson

  • Hamlet has to find proof.
  • Hamlet should not believe the ghost immediately.
  • The law and the Church say that a man must not take private revenge.
  • Hamlet should have killed Claudius when he had the chance.

Common mistakes

WrongRight
Hamlet should to find proof.Hamlet should find proof.
Hamlet have to find proof.Hamlet has to find proof.
He ought find proof.He ought to find proof.
He should acted earlier.He should have acted earlier.

Quick check (2 minutes, hands up or mini whiteboards)Should, has to, must not or should have?

  1. The Ghost orders it: Hamlet ______ avenge his father.
  2. In my opinion, he ______ check the ghost's story.
  3. The Church says a man ______ kill.
  4. He ______ talked to Horatio earlier.
Show the answers

1. has to. 2. should. 3. must not. 4. should have.

Exercises

EntryRecognition. Obligation (O), opinion or advice (A), prohibition (P), criticism of the past (C)?

  1. Hamlet has to obey his father.
  2. He ought to think before he acts.
  3. A son must not kill his king.
  4. Hamlet should have spoken to his mother earlier.
  5. Claudius should confess his crime.
  6. Hamlet shouldn't have killed Polonius.
Show the answers

1. O. 2. A. 3. P. 4. C. 5. A. 6. C.

CoreTransformation. Rewrite with the word in brackets.

  1. It is a good idea for Hamlet to find proof. (should)
  2. The Ghost obliges Hamlet to take revenge. (has to)
  3. Killing is forbidden by the Church. (must not)
  4. It was a mistake not to act during the prayer scene. (should have)
  5. It is right to protect his mother. (ought to)
  6. It was wrong to kill Polonius. (shouldn't have)
  7. He is not obliged to kill: he can wait. (doesn't have to)
Show the answers

1. Hamlet should find proof. 2. Hamlet has to take revenge. 3. A man must not kill. 4. He should have acted during the prayer scene. 5. He ought to protect his mother. 6. He shouldn't have killed Polonius. 7. He doesn't have to kill: he can wait.

StretchProduction. Write the arguments of the dilemma table in six sentences: two for revenge (has to, should), two against (must not, ought to), two judgements on the past (should have, shouldn't have).

Show the answers

For example: Hamlet has to avenge his father, because the Ghost ordered it. He should restore justice in Denmark. However, he must not commit a sin. He ought to find proof first. He should have acted when he was sure. He shouldn't have killed Polonius by mistake.

Going further (for students heading to language studies)Advanced. Modal perfects and formal moral language. Rewrite and explain.

  1. It was not necessary to organise a play. (needn't have)
  2. People expected Hamlet to act quickly. (was supposed to)
  3. Hamlet is obliged by honour to act. (is bound to)
Show the answers

1. Hamlet needn't have organised a play (he did it, but it was not necessary). 2. Hamlet was supposed to act quickly (an expectation he did not meet). 3. Hamlet is bound to act (a strong moral obligation). Needn't have and didn't need to are not the same: the first says the action was done for nothing.

Words in action

To say it precisely, we need the right words

EntryMatch: duty, proof, sin, guilty.

  1. responsible for a crime
  2. evidence that shows the truth
  3. something you must do
  4. an act against religious law
Show the answers

1. guilty. 2. proof. 3. duty. 4. sin.

CoreComplete the dilemma table with: justice, proof, crown. Kill Claudius now: ______ for his father, but no ______. Do nothing: the murderer keeps the ______.

Show the answers

justice, proof, crown.

StretchExplain “conscience” in your own words and give one example.

Show the answers

Conscience is the inner voice that tells us what is good or bad. For example, my conscience stops me from copying a friend's homework.

  2. Language: should, ought to, have to, must not.
  3. Why does Hamlet organise a play to test Claudius? Explain 'catch the conscience of the king'.
  4. Acting troupes: perform a two minute 'play within the play' in modern English.

  2. Turn with 'has to': Hamlet / find proof.

Role play

Student A is Hamlet, Student B is Horatio. Hamlet wants to kill Claudius tonight. Horatio tries to calm him and suggests another way.

Figures of speech in the documents

Metaphor: the play as a trap

“The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king.” (Act II, scene 2, Hamlet)

You catch an animal with a trap; Hamlet wants to “catch” a conscience, something invisible. The play becomes a trap: this is a metaphor. If Claudius reacts to the murder on stage, his guilt will be caught and shown. The two lines also rhyme (thing / king), which makes the plan sound like a magic formula.

EntryWhat do we usually catch?

Show the answers

A ball, a fish, an animal, a thief.

CoreHow will the play “catch” the king's conscience?

Show the answers

The actors show a murder like Claudius's crime; if the king reacts, his guilt will be visible.

StretchFind the rhyme in the two lines and explain its effect.

Show the answers

thing / king: the rhyme closes the scene like a decision or a spell and links the play directly to the king.

  6. The law, not a son, should bring ______.
  7. The ______ within the play shows a murder.
  8. Hamlet wants to catch the ______ of the king.
Answer key
  1. duty
  2. proof
  3. trap
  4. guilty
  5. sin
  6. justice
  7. play
  8. conscience

Expression task

Now say it

Debate: Hamlet must decide. Kill Claudius now, test him with a play, or do nothing?

EntryTwo sentences: your choice with should and one reason.

CoreA one-minute speech: your choice, two arguments, one objection with must not or has to.

StretchAdd a judgement with should have, the metaphor of the trap, and a conclusion.

Tools to use:

  • duty, proof, conscience, sin, justice, guilty, trap
  • should, ought to, has to, must not, should have
  • on the one hand, on the other hand, however
Show a model answer

In my opinion, Hamlet should test Claudius with a play first. On the one hand, he has to avenge his father, because the Ghost ordered it. On the other hand, he must not kill an innocent man: the ghost might be lying. The play is a trap that will catch the king's conscience. Later, of course, he should have acted faster, but at this moment, proof comes first.

Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (I.5): The ghost's line starts with an imperative: “Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder” (I.5). The first word is an order: a dead father gives a command to his living son.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (I.5 and II.2): The father says “foul” and “most unnatural” (I.5). Hamlet says “catch” and “conscience” (II.2). The father judges and condemns; the son prepares a trap and thinks about guilt.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (II.2): Instead of a sword, Hamlet chooses a play: “The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king” (II.2). The rhyme thing / king closes the trap. Hamlet answers violence with theatre: art becomes a weapon against power, a way to make the guilty king show his guilt.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (II.2, then V.2): Hypothesis: if the play catches the king, Hamlet will kill him at once. Partly confirmed: the plan is to “catch the conscience of the king” (II.2), but Hamlet kills Claudius only in the last scene (Act V, scene 2), after many deaths.
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (I.5 and II.2): “Revenge” (I.5) is a sacred duty to the father; “conscience” (II.2) reminds us that the law and the Church condemned private revenge. Hamlet is caught between two laws: the duty to his father and the sin of killing. His conscience is his weapon and his obstacle.

  2. should
  3. must not
  4. should have

Lesson 3: Madness: real or performed?

Part 3. Is Hamlet mad, or does he only act mad?

Objectives

  • Analyse a character's ambiguity
  • Use reported speech
  • Distinguish appearance and reality
Today's language goal

To discuss whether Hamlet is mad or only pretends, and report what the characters say, we need the words of appearance (mask, pretend, madness, method, appearance, reality) and reported speech (Polonius said that there was method in Hamlet's madness).

Getting started

Show a mask. Is a person who wears a mask lying? Students give examples of people who hide their feelings.

Documents

"Though this be madness, yet there is method in't."
William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act II, scene 2, Polonius
Document: two madnesses. Hamlet says he will 'put an antic disposition on': he will pretend to be strange. Ophelia, whose father Polonius is killed by Hamlet, really loses her mind: she sings, gives flowers and drowns.
"Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio"
William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act V, scene 1, Hamlet

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 3: Madness: real or performed?

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act II, scene 2, and Act V, scene 1

  • “Though this be madness, yet there is method in't.” (Act II, scene 2, Polonius)
  • “Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio” (Act V, scene 1, Hamlet)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeII.2What strikes you first?
Two opposite words in one line: “Though this be madness, yet there is method in't” (II.2).
Even Polonius suspects that there is a plan behind the strange words.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesII.2 and the documentWhich clues? In which line?
Hamlet says he will “put an antic disposition on” (document): he will pretend to be strange. Polonius sees “method” (II.2).
The madness is a costume that Hamlet puts on, like an actor: a mask to hide his plan from a court of spies.
Quote each clue with its act and scene.
3 Je comprends · I understandDocument: OpheliaWhat effect? What contrast?
Hamlet performs madness; Ophelia, whose father is killed by Hamlet, really loses her mind: she sings, gives flowers and drowns (document).
The contrast is cruel: Hamlet's mask protects him, but the real victim is Ophelia. A performed madness leads to a real one.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictV.1What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: at the end, Hamlet has become really mad.
Not confirmed: in the graveyard he says “Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio” (V.1). He remembers a friend and thinks calmly about death: he is lucid.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningII.2 and V.1Which interpretation do I defend?
“There is method in't” (II.2) and the lucid voice of “Alas, poor Yorick!” (V.1).
Madness is Hamlet's way to tell the truth in a world of lies: the play asks where fiction ends and reality begins.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … scene … This shows me … because …”

Grammar lesson: reported speech: said that, told, asked if

To discuss whether Hamlet is mad or only pretends, and report what the characters say, we need reported speech: said that, told, asked if
For the teacher: how to run it (8 to 10 minutes)
  1. Read Polonius's line. Ask: what did Polonius say? Write the student answer, then the correct reported version.
  2. Build the table of tense changes on the board: is to was, will to would, can to could, present perfect to past perfect. Add said / told / asked. Students copy.
  3. Show the change of pronouns and time words (now to then, here to there).
  4. Quick check, then exercises, then the comparison of Hamlet and Ophelia.
On the board, to copy

Rule

To report what someone said, use said (that) or told + person, and move the tenses one step back into the past. Change the pronouns and time words. For questions, use asked if / whether or a question word, with normal word order.

Form

  • is / are to was / were; present simple to past simple
  • will to would; can to could
  • past simple or present perfect to past perfect
  • questions: asked if + subject + verb: She asked if he was mad.

Use

  • To tell the story of a scene in a summary.
  • To compare what characters say with what they do.
  • In an essay, to quote without quotation marks.

Examples from the lesson

  • Polonius said that there was method in Hamlet's madness.
  • Hamlet said that he would put an antic disposition on.
  • Hamlet told Horatio that he had known Yorick.
  • Ophelia asked if Hamlet loved her.

Common mistakes

WrongRight
Polonius said me that Hamlet was mad.Polonius told me that Hamlet was mad.
Hamlet said that he will act strangely.Hamlet said that he would act strangely.
She asked if was he mad.She asked if he was mad.
He told that he was sad.He said that he was sad.

Quick check (2 minutes, hands up or mini whiteboards)Report.

  1. Polonius: “Hamlet is mad.”
  2. Hamlet: “I will act strangely.”
  3. Gertrude: “Are you mad?” (to Hamlet)
Show the answers

1. Polonius said that Hamlet was mad. 2. Hamlet said that he would act strangely. 3. Gertrude asked Hamlet if he was mad.

Exercises

EntryRecognition. Find the original words.

  1. Polonius said that there was method in Hamlet's madness.

  5. Claudius asked what Hamlet wanted.

Show the answers

CoreTransformation. Put into reported speech with the verb given.

  1. Hamlet: “I am not mad.” (said)
  2. Polonius to Claudius: “I have found the cause of his madness.” (told)
  3. Claudius: “Hamlet is dangerous.” (said)
  4. Ophelia to Hamlet: “Do you love me?” (asked)
  5. Hamlet: “I will catch the king.” (said)
  6. Gertrude: “Ophelia drowned.” (said)
  7. Horatio to Hamlet: “Can you trust the ghost?” (asked)
  8. Laertes: “I want revenge.” (said)
Show the answers

1. Hamlet said that he was not mad. 2. Polonius told Claudius that he had found the cause of Hamlet's madness. 3. Claudius said that Hamlet was dangerous. 4. Ophelia asked Hamlet if he loved her. 5. Hamlet said that he would catch the king. 6. Gertrude said that Ophelia had drowned. 7. Horatio asked Hamlet if he could trust the ghost. 8. Laertes said that he wanted revenge.

StretchProduction. Write a short report (six sentences) of a meeting at court about Hamlet's strange behaviour: who said what, who asked what.

Show the answers

For example: Claudius asked Polonius what was wrong with Hamlet. Polonius said that the prince was mad with love. Gertrude said that she was worried. Claudius told Polonius to watch Hamlet. Polonius said that there was method in his madness. Finally, the king said that he would send Hamlet to England.

Going further (for students heading to language studies)Advanced. Use reporting verbs instead of say. Rewrite with the verb given.

  1. Hamlet: “I'll pretend to be mad.” (announce)
  2. Claudius: “Go to England.” (order + to)
  3. Polonius: “I didn't know Hamlet was dangerous.” (admit + -ing)
  4. Laertes: “I'll kill Hamlet.” (threaten + to)
Show the answers

1. Hamlet announced that he would pretend to be mad. 2. Claudius ordered Hamlet to go to England. 3. Polonius admitted not knowing that Hamlet was dangerous. 4. Laertes threatened to kill Hamlet. Reporting verbs show the speaker's intention, not only the words, which is essential in literary analysis.

Words in action

To say it precisely, we need the right words

  1. what seems to be
  2. logic, a plan

Show the answers

1. appearance. 2. method. 3. madness. 4. pretend.

CoreSort into two columns, appearance or reality: a mask, the truth, to pretend, a feeling hidden inside, a role, what really happened.

Show the answers

Appearance: a mask, to pretend, a role. Reality: the truth, a feeling hidden inside, what really happened.

StretchExplain “an antic disposition” in your own words.

Show the answers

A strange, crazy way of behaving that Hamlet chooses to show, like a mask, to hide his plans.

Role play

Student A is Polonius, Student B is King Claudius. Polonius explains why Hamlet is mad. Claudius is suspicious.

Figures of speech in the documents

Paradox: “method in madness”

“Though this be madness, yet there is method in't.” (Act II, scene 2, Polonius)

Madness means loss of reason; method means logic. Saying that madness has a method seems absurd but hides a truth: Hamlet's strange words follow a plan. This is a paradox, built on an antithesis (madness / method). The phrase “method in madness” is still used in English today.

EntryWhich two words are opposites in Polonius's line?

Show the answers

madness and method.

CoreWhat does Polonius understand about Hamlet with this paradox?

Show the answers

That Hamlet's madness may be a mask: his strange words follow a plan.

StretchUse “there is method in his madness” about a modern person, and explain.

Show the answers

For example: My brother's room looks chaotic, but there is method in his madness: he knows where everything is.

Now say it

Write a paragraph: is Hamlet mad, or does he only act mad? Compare him with Ophelia.

EntryThree sentences: your answer, one reported sentence, one reason.

CoreTen lines: your answer, two arguments with reported speech, a comparison with Ophelia.

StretchUse two reporting verbs, the paradox “method in madness” and a nuance.

Tools to use:

  • mask, pretend, madness, method, appearance, reality
  • said that, told, asked if; announced, admitted
  • whereas, however, while
Show a model answer

In my opinion, Hamlet only pretends to be mad. In Act I he announced that he would put an antic disposition on, so his madness is a mask. Even Polonius said that there was method in his madness. However, the mask becomes dangerous: Hamlet kills Polonius and loses control. Whereas Hamlet chooses his madness, Ophelia really loses her mind: she is a victim, not an actor.

Lesson 3: Madness: real or performed?. Your lesson at home or in hospital, about 40 minutes, at your own pace. Stop when you are tired: you can do it in two parts.

  1. Read the key lines aloud, slowly, twice:
    • “Though this be madness, yet there is method in't.” (Act II, scene 2, Polonius)
    • “Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio” (Act V, scene 1, Hamlet)
  2. Learn the eight words of the Vocabulary box of the lesson.
  3. Do the spirale de Gorse: copy the five steps on your worksheet (or use the worksheet of this lesson). For each step, write one idea and one line from the text. Then check below.
  4. Quick check: Report.
    • Polonius: “Hamlet is mad.”
    • Hamlet: “I will act strangely.”

Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (II.2): Two opposite words in one line: “Though this be madness, yet there is method in't” (II.2). Even Polonius suspects that there is a plan behind the strange words.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (II.2 and the document): Hamlet says he will “put an antic disposition on” (document): he will pretend to be strange. Polonius sees “method” (II.2). The madness is a costume that Hamlet puts on, like an actor: a mask to hide his plan from a court of spies.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Document: Ophelia): Hamlet performs madness; Ophelia, whose father is killed by Hamlet, really loses her mind: she sings, gives flowers and drowns (document). The contrast is cruel: Hamlet's mask protects him, but the real victim is Ophelia. A performed madness leads to a real one.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (V.1): Hypothesis: at the end, Hamlet has become really mad. Not confirmed: in the graveyard he says “Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio” (V.1). He remembers a friend and thinks calmly about death: he is lucid.
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (II.2 and V.1): “There is method in't” (II.2) and the lucid voice of “Alas, poor Yorick!” (V.1). Madness is Hamlet's way to tell the truth in a world of lies: the play asks where fiction ends and reality begins.
Check my quick check
  1. Polonius said that Hamlet was mad.
  2. Hamlet said that he would act strangely.
  3. Gertrude asked Hamlet if he was mad.

Lesson 4: To be or not to be

Part 4. What does Hamlet's most famous speech tell us about the tragic hero?

Objectives

  • Read and analyse a soliloquy
  • Express hypothesis (if, whether)
  • Perform a speech with intonation
Today's language goal

To analyse the soliloquy and express a hypothesis or a dilemma, we need the words of the soliloquy (suffer, fortune, troubles, conscience, coward, soliloquy) and the language of hypothesis: if, whether ... or, unless, what if.

Getting started

Students hear the first line read three ways: angry, sad, calm. Which one works best, and why?

"Thus conscience does make cowards of us all;"

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeIII.1, line 1What strikes you first?
The speech opens on a choice: “To be, or not to be, that is the question” (III.1).
Hamlet is alone in front of the audience and thinks aloud: the hero of action becomes a hero of questions.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesIII.1Which clues? In which line?
“The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune”, “take arms against a sea of troubles”, “To die: to sleep” (III.1).
Life is a battle against fortune; death is softened into sleep. The images show a mind at war with itself.
Quote each clue with its act and scene.
3 Je comprends · I understandIII.1What effect? What contrast?
“Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer” ... “Or to take arms” (III.1).
The grammar of the dilemma (whether ... or) splits the hero in two: to accept or to act.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictIII.1, last lineWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: at the end of the speech, Hamlet decides to act.
Not confirmed: “Thus conscience does make cowards of us all” (III.1). Thinking stops action, and “us all” includes the audience.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningIII.1Which interpretation do I defend?
“To be, or not to be” and “conscience does make cowards of us all” (III.1).
Hamlet's tragic weakness is his lucid hesitation. He speaks for every human being who doubts before acting.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
questionsomething you ask
sufferfeel pain
fortunedestiny, luck

Grammar lesson: hypothesis: if, whether ... or, unless, what if

To analyse the soliloquy and express a hypothesis or a dilemma, we need hypothesis: if, whether ... or, unless, what if
For the teacher: how to run it (8 to 10 minutes)
  1. Read the first line in three ways (getting started). Ask: what is the question? Write “whether to live or to die”.
  2. Show the difference: if introduces a condition; whether ... or presents two options. Write the conditional patterns (real and imaginary). Students copy.
  3. Add unless (= if not) and what if (an open hypothesis).
  4. Quick check, then exercises, then the modern rewriting of the dilemma.
On the board, to copy

Rule

whether ... or presents two possibilities (often after wonder, ask, decide). if introduces a condition: real (if + present, will) or imaginary (if + past, would). unless means if not. What if opens a hypothesis.

Form

  • whether + to + verb / clause + or: He wonders whether to suffer or to fight.
  • real: if + present, will: If he waits, Claudius will escape.
  • imaginary: if + past, would: If death were only a sleep, he would not be afraid.
  • unless + present = if ... not: Unless he acts, nothing will change.

Use

  • To rewrite the dilemma of the soliloquy.
  • To imagine Hamlet's choices and their consequences.
  • In your own soliloquy, to weigh two options.

Examples from the lesson

  • Hamlet wonders whether it is nobler to suffer or to fight.
  • If death were only a sleep, he would not hesitate.
  • Unless he acts, Claudius will keep the crown.
  • What if death is full of bad dreams?

Common mistakes

WrongRight
He wonders if to suffer or to fight.He wonders whether to suffer or to fight.
If he would act, he would win.If he acted, he would win.
Unless he doesn't act, nothing will change.Unless he acts, nothing will change.
If he will wait, Claudius will escape.If he waits, Claudius will escape.

Quick check (2 minutes, hands up or mini whiteboards)If, whether or unless?

  1. Hamlet doesn't know ______ to live or to die.
  2. ______ he acts, nothing will change.
  3. ______ death were only a sleep, he would not be afraid.
Show the answers

1. whether. 2. Unless. 3. If.

Exercises

EntryRecognition. Two options (W), real condition (R), imaginary condition (I) or if not (U)?

  1. He wonders whether to suffer or to fight.
  2. If he waits, Claudius will escape.
  3. If he were braver, he would act.
  4. Unless he finds proof, he will not kill.
  5. Whether he lives or dies, the problem stays.
  6. If death were a dreamless sleep, everyone would choose it.
Show the answers

1. W. 2. R. 3. I. 4. U. 5. W. 6. I.

CoreGap-fill. Complete with whether, or, if, unless and put the verbs in the right form.

  1. Hamlet wonders ______ to suffer ______ to take arms.
  2. If he (fight), he (end) his troubles.
  3. If death (be) only a sleep, it (be) easy.
  4. ______ conscience stops him, he will act.
  5. He asks himself ______ death is the end ______ the beginning of bad dreams.
  6. If he (not / think) so much, he (act) faster.
  7. ______ he decides now, Claudius will win.
Show the answers

1. whether, or. 2. fights, will end. 3. were, would be. 4. Unless. 5. whether, or. 6. didn't think, would act. 7. Unless.

StretchProduction. Rewrite Hamlet's dilemma in modern English in six sentences, with whether, two if-sentences (one real, one imaginary), unless and what if.

Show the answers

For example: I wonder whether I should accept my pain or fight it. If I fight, I might die. If death were only a peaceful sleep, I would not hesitate. But what if death is full of nightmares? Unless I know what comes after, I will keep suffering. So thinking too much makes me a coward.

Going further (for students heading to language studies)Advanced. Inversion and formal hypothesis. Rewrite.

  1. If Hamlet had acted at once, Ophelia would still be alive. (Had ...)
  2. If death were only a sleep, nobody would fear it. (Were ...)
  3. If he should find proof, he will act. (Should ...)
  4. Suppose that death is a dream: what then?
Show the answers

1. Had Hamlet acted at once, Ophelia would still be alive. 2. Were death only a sleep, nobody would fear it. 3. Should he find proof, he will act. 4. For example: Supposing death were a dream, would we dare to die? Inversion is formal and literary, close to Shakespeare's own “Whether 'tis nobler”.

Words in action

1. soliloquy. 2. coward. 3. fortune. 4. suffer.

the attacks of a cruel destiny; to fight against all one's problems.

Show the answers

Because sleep is peaceful: if death is only sleep, it ends pain without fear.

  2. Cruel, unfair destiny.

Role play

Student A is Hamlet, Student B is his inner voice. Hamlet hesitates; the voice pushes him to act. Then swap.

Figures of speech in the documents

Metaphors of suffering: slings and arrows, a sea of troubles, death as sleep

“The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, / Or to take arms against a sea of troubles” “To die: to sleep” (Act III, scene 1, Hamlet)

Fortune shoots at us like an archer: slings and arrows is a metaphor of attack. Our problems become an ocean: a sea of troubles, immense and endless. Fighting the sea with weapons is impossible, which shows that the fight is hopeless (critics call this a mixed metaphor). To die: to sleep is a metaphor and a euphemism: death is presented as a gentle sleep.

EntryWhat is compared to a sea?

Show the answers

Hamlet's troubles, his problems.

CoreWhy is it absurd to “take arms” against a sea? What does it show?

Show the answers

Weapons cannot stop the sea: the image shows that fighting fate seems hopeless.

StretchWrite two lines of your own soliloquy with a metaphor of attack and a metaphor of water.

Show the answers

For example: Exams fire their arrows every Monday, and I am drowning in an ocean of homework.

To speak or not to speak, that is my question. I wonder whether I should tell my friend the truth or keep quiet. If I tell her, she will be angry. If I kept the secret, I would carry a sea of guilt. Unless I speak now, the lie will grow. What if silence is the real coward's choice?

Lesson 5: The tragic end

Part 5. Why does everybody die, and what remains?

Objectives

  • Understand the ending and the tragic
  • Write a short critical paragraph
  • Prepare the final task
Today's language goal

To explain the ending and write a critical paragraph on the tragic, we need the words of tragedy (fate, weakness, pity, fear, wounded, poisoned) and linking words of cause, consequence, contrast and concession.

Getting started

Students list endings of films they know: happy, sad, tragic. What is the difference between sad and tragic?

Documents

Document: what is the tragic? In a tragedy, a noble hero faces a fate he cannot escape. He often has a weakness (Aristotle called it hamartia). The audience feels pity and fear. The end is death, but the hero gains a kind of lucidity before it.
Document: the last scene. A fencing match between Hamlet and Laertes is a trap. The sword is poisoned, the wine too. Gertrude drinks, Laertes and Hamlet are wounded, Hamlet kills Claudius. Dying, he asks Horatio to tell his story.
"The rest is silence."
William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act V, scene 2, Hamlet

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 5: The tragic end

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act V, scene 2, with the document “The last scene”

  • “The rest is silence.” (Act V, scene 2, Hamlet)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeV.2What strikes you first?
Hamlet's last words are very short: “The rest is silence” (V.2).
After a play full of words, speeches and puns, the hero ends with silence.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesDocument: the last sceneWhich clues? In which line?
“The sword is poisoned, the wine too”; Gertrude drinks, Laertes and Hamlet are wounded, Hamlet kills Claudius (document).
Poison links the end to the beginning: the old king was poisoned too (lesson 1).
Quote each clue with its act and scene.
3 Je comprends · I understandV.2 and the documentWhat effect? What contrast?
Hamlet says “The rest is silence” (V.2), but he asks Horatio to tell his story (document).
The hero falls silent, but memory goes on: it answers the ghost's “remember me” (I.5).
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictI.5 and V.2What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: the end will repeat the murder of the beginning.
Confirmed: the ghost was poisoned (I.5), and at the end “the sword is poisoned, the wine too”. Revenge is done, but everybody pays for it.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningV.2Which interpretation do I defend?
A noble hero, a weakness (hesitation, the hamartia), a fate he cannot escape, pity and fear, and a last lucidity: “The rest is silence” (V.2).
Hamlet dies, but his story survives: the tragic turns death into memory and makes the audience think.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … scene … This shows me … because …”

Grammar lesson: linking words for a critical paragraph

To explain the ending and write a critical paragraph on the tragic, we need linking words for a critical paragraph
For the teacher: how to run it (8 to 10 minutes)
  1. Ask: why does everybody die? Collect answers, then show how to link them: because of the trap, so, however.
  2. Build the table of linking words on the board: cause, consequence, contrast, concession, addition. Students copy with one example each.
  3. Show the structure of a critical paragraph: point, evidence (quotation), explanation, link.
  4. Quick check, then exercises, then the paragraph.
On the board, to copy

Rule

A critical paragraph links ideas with precise words. Cause: because, since, because of + noun. Consequence: so, therefore, as a result. Contrast: whereas, while, however. Concession: although + clause, despite + noun or -ing.

Form

  • because + subject + verb; because of + noun: because of his hesitation
  • therefore / as a result, at the start of a sentence, with a comma
  • although + subject + verb; despite + noun / -ing: despite his courage
  • whereas joins two contrasting clauses: Hamlet hesitates, whereas Laertes acts.

Use

  • To explain the chain of deaths in the last scene.
  • To link the ending to the definition of the tragic.
  • To write the critical paragraph and the final task.

Examples from the lesson

  • Hamlet dies because of a poisoned sword.
  • Hamlet hesitates for a long time; as a result, many innocent people die.
  • Although he dies, Hamlet gains a kind of lucidity.
  • Hamlet hesitates, whereas Laertes acts at once.

Common mistakes

WrongRight
Because of he hesitates, he dies.Because he hesitates, he dies.
Despite he is brave, he dies.Although he is brave, he dies. / Despite his courage, he dies.
Although he is noble, but he dies.Although he is noble, he dies.
Therefore he dies. (without a comma at the start)Therefore, he dies.

Quick check (2 minutes, hands up or mini whiteboards)Choose the right linking word.

  1. Hamlet dies (because / because of) a poisoned sword.
  2. (Although / Despite) his courage, he cannot escape his fate.
  3. Hamlet hesitates, (whereas / therefore) Laertes acts at once.
  4. The wine is poisoned; (as a result / although), Gertrude dies.
Show the answers

1. because of. 2. Despite. 3. whereas. 4. as a result.

Exercises

EntryRecognition. Cause (C), consequence (R), contrast (O) or concession (N)?

  1. Hamlet dies because of his hesitation.
  2. Therefore, the audience feels pity.
  3. Although he is noble, he has a weakness.
  4. Claudius wants the crown, whereas Hamlet wants the truth.
  5. Despite his intelligence, he cannot escape his fate.
  6. As a result, Horatio is the only survivor.
Show the answers

1. C. 2. R. 3. N. 4. O. 5. N. 6. R.

CoreJoin the two sentences with the word given.

  1. Hamlet is noble. He has a weakness. (although)
  2. Hamlet hesitates. Many people die. (as a result)
  3. The sword is poisoned. Laertes dies too. (because)
  4. Hamlet is intelligent. He makes fatal mistakes. (despite)
  5. Hamlet thinks. Laertes acts. (whereas)
  6. The hero dies. The audience feels pity and fear. (therefore)
  7. Hamlet wants proof. He organises a play. (since)
Show the answers

1. Although Hamlet is noble, he has a weakness. 2. Hamlet hesitates; as a result, many people die. 3. Laertes dies too because the sword is poisoned. 4. Despite his intelligence, Hamlet makes fatal mistakes. 5. Hamlet thinks, whereas Laertes acts. 6. The hero dies; therefore, the audience feels pity and fear. 7. Since Hamlet wants proof, he organises a play.

StretchProduction. Write a critical paragraph of eight to ten lines: Is Hamlet guilty, a victim, or both? Use five different linking words and one quotation.

Show the answers

For example: Hamlet is both guilty and a victim. On the one hand, he is a victim of fate, because his uncle murdered his father and the Ghost imposed revenge. On the other hand, his weakness, his hesitation, causes many deaths; as a result, Polonius, Ophelia and Gertrude die. Although he finally kills Claudius, it is too late. His last words, “The rest is silence”, show that he accepts his end. Therefore, he is a true tragic hero: we feel pity and fear for him.

Going further (for students heading to language studies)Advanced. Use nominal linkers and inversion for a formal style. Rewrite.

  1. Because Hamlet hesitated, Ophelia died. (owing to + noun)
  2. Although he is lucid, he cannot escape. (lucid as he is, ...)
  3. Hamlet did not only kill Claudius; he also lost his own life. (Not only ...)
  4. Many critics see a weakness in his hesitation. (hamartia: explain)
Show the answers

1. Owing to Hamlet's hesitation, Ophelia died. 2. Lucid as he is, he cannot escape. 3. Not only did Hamlet kill Claudius, but he also lost his own life. 4. For example: Many critics see in his hesitation Hamlet's hamartia, the tragic weakness Aristotle describes, which leads a noble hero to his fall.

A sad story makes us unhappy; a tragic story shows a noble hero who cannot escape his fate, and it makes us feel pity and fear.

Figures of speech in the documents

Euphemism and pun: “The rest is silence”

“The rest is silence.” (Act V, scene 2, Hamlet)

Hamlet does not say “I am dying”: he says silence, a gentle way of naming death. This is a euphemism. The word rest also has two meanings: the remainder (everything else) and repose (sleep, peace). This double meaning is a pun: what remains is silence, and death is at last a rest, which recalls “To die: to sleep” in the soliloquy.

EntryWhich word replaces “death” in Hamlet's last line?

Show the answers

silence.

CoreGive the two meanings of “rest”.

Show the answers

the remainder (everything that is left) and repose (sleep, peace).

StretchLink “The rest is silence” to “To die: to sleep”. What has changed for Hamlet?

Show the answers

In Act III, he feared what comes after sleep; at the end, he accepts death calmly as rest: he has gained a kind of lucidity.

Expression task

Now say it

Write a short critical paragraph: Why does everybody die, and what remains?

EntryFour sentences with because, so and but, and one quotation.

CoreTen lines: point, evidence, explanation, link to the tragic, with four linking words.

StretchUse although, despite and whereas, the word hamartia, and the pun on “rest”.

Tools to use:

  • fate, weakness, pity, fear, poisoned, wounded
  • because of, as a result, although, despite, whereas
  • point, evidence, explanation, link
Show a model answer

Everybody dies because of a trap: the sword and the wine are poisoned. As a result, the guilty and the innocent fall together, Gertrude and Laertes as well as Claudius. Although Hamlet finally kills the king, his hesitation, his hamartia, has made the catastrophe inevitable. What remains is Horatio, who will tell the story, and Hamlet's last words: “The rest is silence”. The audience feels pity and fear, which is the definition of the tragic.

  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (V.2): Hamlet's last words are very short: “The rest is silence” (V.2). After a play full of words, speeches and puns, the hero ends with silence.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Document: the last scene): “The sword is poisoned, the wine too”; Gertrude drinks, Laertes and Hamlet are wounded, Hamlet kills Claudius (document). Poison links the end to the beginning: the old king was poisoned too (lesson 1).
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (V.2 and the document): Hamlet says “The rest is silence” (V.2), but he asks Horatio to tell his story (document). The hero falls silent, but memory goes on: it answers the ghost's “remember me” (I.5).
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (I.5 and V.2): Hypothesis: the end will repeat the murder of the beginning. Confirmed: the ghost was poisoned (I.5), and at the end “the sword is poisoned, the wine too”. Revenge is done, but everybody pays for it.
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (V.2): A noble hero, a weakness (hesitation, the hamartia), a fate he cannot escape, pity and fear, and a last lucidity: “The rest is silence” (V.2). Hamlet dies, but his story survives: the tragic turns death into memory and makes the audience think.

Teacher notes

A very flexible sequence. This Hamlet sequence is highly flexible: every lesson stands alone, lessons can be shortened, merged or reordered, and the documents can be swapped between the versions.

GEREX

Each lesson follows the GEREX logic: students Generate ideas (getting started), Explore a document, Reformulate it in their own words, EXercise the language point, then reuse it in a short task. The worksheet and the homework close the loop.

Differentiated pedagogy

  • Four versions: Première and Terminale (lycée général et technologique), Version B (bac pro) and the Dys-friendly version, for students with dyslexia or reading difficulties. Each lesson also has a route for students who cannot come to class or are in hospital.
  • Sentence starters on every page for students who need support.
  • Extension tasks for strong students.
  • Role plays in pairs or small groups, with roles of different difficulty.

Lesson 1: The ghost on the walls

Part 1. Why is a ghost the perfect start for a tragedy?

Objectives

  • Discover the plot and the characters
  • Describe a supernatural scene
  • Use modals of deduction (must, might, can't)
Today's language goal

To present the play and its characters and describe a supernatural scene, we need the words of the plot (ghost, revenge, crown, poison, court, castle) and the modals of deduction (The ghost must be his father).

Getting started

Lights off. Students hear the word ghost and list everything it suggests: fear, the past, unfinished business. Why do ghosts come back in stories?

Documents

Document: the play. Hamlet is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, written around 1600. Prince Hamlet of Denmark comes home after his father's death. His uncle Claudius is now king and has married Hamlet's mother, Gertrude. A ghost appears on the walls of the castle of Elsinore: it is Hamlet's father, who says Claudius poisoned him. Hamlet must decide whether to believe the ghost and take revenge. At the end, almost all the main characters die: Polonius, Ophelia, Laertes, Gertrude, Claudius and Hamlet himself. Only his friend Horatio survives to tell the story.

"Something is rotten in the state of Denmark."

"I am thy father's spirit, Doom'd for a certain term to walk the night"

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 1: The ghost on the walls

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act I, scenes 4 and 5

  • “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.” (Act I, scene 4, Marcellus)
  • “I am thy father's spirit, / Doom'd for a certain term to walk the night” (Act I, scene 5, the Ghost)
  • “Adieu, adieu, adieu! remember me.” (Act I, scene 5, the Ghost)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeI.4 and I.5What strikes you first?
A dead king speaks: “I am thy father's spirit” (I.5). Before that, a guard says: “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark” (I.4).
The play opens on something wrong, in the royal family and in the whole country.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesI.5Which clues? In which line?
“Doom'd for a certain term to walk the night” (I.5) and “remember me” (I.5), with “Adieu” said three times.
The words of night and doom make the ghost a messenger from death. His last wish is not only revenge: it is memory.
Quote each clue with its act and scene.
3 Je comprends · I understandI.4What effect? What contrast?
“Something is rotten in the state of Denmark” (I.4): a country cannot rot like fruit or meat.
The metaphor turns a secret crime into a public disease: the corruption at the top of the state will spread to everything.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictI.5, then II.2What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: Hamlet will obey the ghost and take revenge immediately.
Not confirmed: the ghost asks “remember me” (I.5), and in Act II Hamlet still wants proof: “The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king” (II.2).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningI.4 and I.5Which interpretation do I defend?
The ghost brings a secret from death into the court: “Something is rotten” (I.4), “remember me” (I.5).
From the first act, the hero is trapped between memory and action, between a duty and a doubt: this is where the tragic begins.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … scene … This shows me … because …”

Grammar lesson: modals of deduction: must, might, can't (present and past)

To present the play and its characters and describe a supernatural scene, we need modals of deduction: must, might, can't (present and past)
For the teacher: how to run it (8 to 10 minutes)
  1. Read “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark”. Ask: what does Marcellus suspect? Collect guesses.
  2. Draw the certainty line: can't (no), might / could (maybe), must (yes). Students copy.
  3. Add the past: must have + past participle. “Claudius must have poisoned the king.” Ask what the clue is.
  4. Quick check, then exercises, then the character chart and the role play.
On the board, to copy

Rule

To make a guess from clues, use a modal + base verb for now, and a modal + have + past participle for the past. must = almost sure; might / could = possible; can't = almost sure it is not true.

Form

  • now: modal + base verb: The ghost must be Hamlet's father.
  • past: modal + have + past participle: Claudius must have poisoned him.
  • the negative of must (deduction) is can't: It can't be a dream.
  • questions: Could the ghost be lying?

Use

  • To talk about the ghost: real or imagined, honest or lying?
  • To guess what happened before the play starts.
  • Always add the clue: because, since, so.

Examples from the lesson

  • The ghost must be Hamlet's father: it wears his armour.
  • Claudius must have poisoned the king, if the ghost says the truth.
  • The ghost might be a devil who wants to trick Hamlet.
  • It can't be a dream: the guards saw it too.

Common mistakes

WrongRight
The ghost must to be his father.The ghost must be his father.
It mustn't be a dream.It can't be a dream.
Claudius must poisoned the king.Claudius must have poisoned the king.
Can the ghost lie? (deduction)Could the ghost be lying?

Quick check (2 minutes, hands up or mini whiteboards)Must, might or can't?

  1. The guards saw it too: it ______ be a dream.
  2. The ghost wears the king's armour: it ______ be the king.
  3. We have no proof: the ghost ______ be lying.
  4. Claudius ______ have killed his brother: the ghost says so.
Show the answers

1. can't. 2. must. 3. might. 4. must (or might, if we doubt the ghost).

Exercises

EntryRecognition. How sure is the speaker: yes (Y), maybe (M), no (N)? Now or past?

  1. Something must be wrong in Denmark.
  2. The ghost might be a devil.
  3. Claudius must have poisoned the king.
  4. Hamlet can't be happy about the wedding.
  5. Gertrude might not have known about the murder.
  6. It can't have been an accident.
Show the answers

1. Y, now. 2. M, now. 3. Y, past. 4. N, now. 5. M, past. 6. N, past.

CoreTransformation. Rewrite with must, might or can't (present or past).

  1. I'm sure the ghost is the old king.
  2. Perhaps Horatio is afraid.
  3. I'm sure Hamlet isn't happy at court.
  4. I'm sure Claudius killed his brother.
  5. Perhaps Gertrude didn't know.
  6. I'm sure it wasn't a natural death.
  7. Maybe the ghost is telling the truth.
Show the answers

1. The ghost must be the old king. 2. Horatio might be afraid. 3. Hamlet can't be happy at court. 4. Claudius must have killed his brother. 5. Gertrude might not have known. 6. It can't have been a natural death. 7. The ghost might be telling the truth.

StretchProduction. You are a guard on the walls. Write five deductions about the ghost and the king's death, each with a clue.

Show the answers

For example: The ghost wears the king's armour, so it must be the dead king. It only appears at night: it might be a spirit from purgatory. It can't be a dream, because three of us saw it. The king died suddenly; someone must have poisoned him. Claudius married the queen very fast: he might have planned everything.

Going further (for students heading to language studies)Advanced. Use the continuous and passive forms of deduction. Rewrite.

  1. Perhaps the ghost is waiting for Hamlet. (continuous)
  2. I'm sure someone poured poison into his ear. (passive past)
  3. I'm sure Hamlet has not been sleeping. (can't + continuous perfect)
Show the answers

1. The ghost might be waiting for Hamlet. 2. Poison must have been poured into his ear. 3. Hamlet can't have been sleeping. Continuous and passive forms let a critic make precise guesses about action and responsibility.

Role play

Figures of speech in the documents

Metaphor: “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark”

“Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.” (Act I, scene 4, Marcellus)

A country cannot rot like fruit or meat: Marcellus compares Denmark to a body or a food that is going bad. This is a metaphor. It suggests a hidden corruption at the top of the state (the murder, the hasty marriage) which will spread to everything.

EntryWhat can be rotten in real life?

Show the answers

Food, fruit, meat, wood.

CoreWhat is rotten in Denmark, in fact?

Show the answers

The power: the king was murdered by his brother, who now sits on the throne and has married the queen.

StretchUse the same metaphor to describe a modern situation, then explain it.

Show the answers

For example: Something is rotten in this club: the best players never play. The metaphor suggests a hidden problem that spoils the whole group.

Expression task

Now say it

Role play: two guards on the walls of Elsinore at midnight see the ghost.

EntryEach guard says two sentences, one with must, might or can't.

CoreTwo minutes: describe the ghost, make three deductions, decide to tell Hamlet.

StretchUse a past deduction (must have) and the metaphor “something is rotten”.

Tools to use:

  • ghost, revenge, crown, poison, castle, walls
  • must, might, can't; must have + participle
  • because, so
Show a model answer

A: Look, over there! It must be the old king: it wears his armour. B: It can't be a dream; Horatio saw it too. A: It might be a devil who wants to trick us. B: Or the king must have something to say. Something is rotten in the state of Denmark. A: We must tell Prince Hamlet tonight.

Terminale LV1 · C1/C2 extension track

For strong or anglophone students. Here the ghost is read as a problem of knowledge: can Hamlet trust what he sees?

Extended extract

The spirit that I have seen
May be a devil, and the devil hath power
To assume a pleasing shape; yea, and perhaps
Out of my weakness and my melancholy,
As he is very potent with such spirits,
Abuses me to damn me. I'll have grounds
More relative than this.
William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act II, scene 2 (public domain)

Critical analysis

  1. How does Hamlet turn a ghost story into a question of evidence?
  2. What does 'out of my weakness and my melancholy' reveal about his self awareness?
  3. Is his doubt prudence or an excuse for delay? Justify with the text.

Argued writing (C1: 300 words · C2: 400 words)

Essay: 'Hamlet's tragedy begins not with murder but with uncertainty.' Discuss.

Debate

Motion: This house believes Hamlet is justified in doubting the ghost. Two teams, opening speeches of one minute, rebuttals, then an open floor.

Homework

Write the diary of Horatio after the night on the walls (120 words, three modals of deduction).

If a student cannot attend class or is in hospital

Lesson 1: The ghost on the walls. Your lesson at home or in hospital, about 40 minutes, at your own pace. Stop when you are tired: you can do it in two parts.

  1. Read the key lines aloud, slowly, twice:
    • “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.” (Act I, scene 4, Marcellus)
    • “I am thy father's spirit, / Doom'd for a certain term to walk the night” (Act I, scene 5, the Ghost)
    • “Adieu, adieu, adieu! remember me.” (Act I, scene 5, the Ghost)
  2. Learn the eight words of the Vocabulary box of the lesson.
  3. Do the spirale de Gorse: copy the five steps on your worksheet (or use the worksheet of this lesson). For each step, write one idea and one line from the text. Then check below.
  4. Quick check: Must, might or can't?
    • The guards saw it too: it ______ be a dream.
    • The ghost wears the king's armour: it ______ be the king.
    • We have no proof: the ghost ______ be lying.
    • Claudius ______ have killed his brother: the ghost says so.
  5. Send to your teacher through the school’s online messaging: record one minute (audio) as a guard on the walls: describe the ghost and make three deductions (must, might, can't).
Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (I.4 and I.5): A dead king speaks: “I am thy father's spirit” (I.5). Before that, a guard says: “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark” (I.4). The play opens on something wrong, in the royal family and in the whole country.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (I.5): “Doom'd for a certain term to walk the night” (I.5) and “remember me” (I.5), with “Adieu” said three times. The words of night and doom make the ghost a messenger from death. His last wish is not only revenge: it is memory.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (I.4): “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark” (I.4): a country cannot rot like fruit or meat. The metaphor turns a secret crime into a public disease: the corruption at the top of the state will spread to everything.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (I.5, then II.2): Hypothesis: Hamlet will obey the ghost and take revenge immediately. Not confirmed: the ghost asks “remember me” (I.5), and in Act II Hamlet still wants proof: “The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king” (II.2).
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (I.4 and I.5): The ghost brings a secret from death into the court: “Something is rotten” (I.4), “remember me” (I.5). From the first act, the hero is trapped between memory and action, between a duty and a doubt: this is where the tragic begins.
Check my quick check
  1. can't
  2. must
  3. might
  4. must

Lesson 2: Revenge: duty or crime?

Part 2. Should Hamlet obey the ghost?

Objectives

  • Understand the revenge tragedy
  • Express obligation and moral judgment
  • Debate with arguments
Today's language goal

To weigh the arguments for and against revenge and give my judgement, we need the words of moral choice (duty, proof, conscience, sin, justice, guilty, trap) and should, ought to, have to, must not (and should have to judge the past).

Getting started

Vote with your feet: one side of the room for 'revenge is justice', the other for 'revenge is a crime'. Explain your choice in one sentence.

Documents

"Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder."
William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act I, scene 5, the Ghost
Document: revenge tragedy. In Elizabethan England, revenge plays were very popular. The law and the Church condemned private revenge, so the hero is caught between a sacred duty to his father and a sin.
"The play's the thing Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king."
William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act II, scene 2, Hamlet

Dilemma table

ChoiceForAgainst
Kill Claudius nowjustice for his fatherno proof, it is a sin
Test him with a playproof firsttime lost, danger
Do nothingno crimethe murderer keeps the crown

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 2: Revenge: duty or crime?

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act I, scene 5, and Act II, scene 2

  • “Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder.” (Act I, scene 5, the Ghost)
  • “The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king.” (Act II, scene 2, Hamlet)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeI.5What strikes you first?
The ghost's line starts with an imperative: “Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder” (I.5).
The first word is an order: a dead father gives a command to his living son.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesI.5 and II.2Which clues? In which line?
The father says “foul” and “most unnatural” (I.5). Hamlet says “catch” and “conscience” (II.2).
The father judges and condemns; the son prepares a trap and thinks about guilt.
Quote each clue with its act and scene.
3 Je comprends · I understandII.2What effect? What contrast?
Instead of a sword, Hamlet chooses a play: “The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king” (II.2). The rhyme thing / king closes the trap.
Hamlet answers violence with theatre: art becomes a weapon against power, a way to make the guilty king show his guilt.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictII.2, then V.2What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: if the play catches the king, Hamlet will kill him at once.
Partly confirmed: the plan is to “catch the conscience of the king” (II.2), but Hamlet kills Claudius only in the last scene (Act V, scene 2), after many deaths.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningI.5 and II.2Which interpretation do I defend?
“Revenge” (I.5) is a sacred duty to the father; “conscience” (II.2) reminds us that the law and the Church condemned private revenge.
Hamlet is caught between two laws: the duty to his father and the sin of killing. His conscience is his weapon and his obstacle.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … scene … This shows me … because …”

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
